questions.stem: The Defence Act 1909 introduced which change to Australian defence?
options: Compulsory military training for boys and young men in peacetime
Conscription of adult men for service with the British Army overseas
A permanent standing army that replaced the colonial militias
Voluntary enlistment in a new Australian Imperial Force for overseas service
questions.explanation: The 1909 Act, which took effect from 1911, made military training compulsory for boys and young men, organised as junior and senior cadets and then the citizen forces. It was about home defence: the Defence Act did not allow conscripts to be sent overseas.

questions.stem: In 1914 the AIF had to be raised from volunteers. Why?
options: The Defence Act did not allow conscripts to be compelled to serve overseas
The Constitution required a referendum before any war could be formally declared
Britain had asked the dominions to send only volunteers to Europe
The compulsory training scheme had been repealed by the Fisher government
questions.explanation: Australia's defence law limited compulsory service to the defence of Australia and its territories, so a force for overseas service had to be voluntary. This is why Hughes later sought popular approval to conscript men for overseas service.

questions.stem: How did Australia come to be at war in August 1914?
options: Australia declared war after German ships attacked Australian ports
The governor-general declared war after a request from the French government
Britain's declaration of war bound the whole Empire, including Australia
The federal parliament voted to declare war on Germany after a long debate
questions.explanation: Britain's declaration of war on 4 August 1914 committed the whole Empire, and Australia had no separate power to stay out. Both major parties pledged full support during the 1914 election campaign.

questions.stem: During the 1914 election campaign, Labor leader Andrew Fisher pledged that Australia would support Britain 'to our last man and our last shilling'. What does this pledge best show?
options: Fisher's plan to introduce conscription if he won government
A demand that Britain pay for the troops Australia would send
Bipartisan support for the war rooted in loyalty to the Empire
Labor's early opposition to sending Australian troops overseas
questions.explanation: Fisher's pledge matched the Liberal government's support for Britain, showing how widely loyalty to the Empire was shared in 1914. Labor did not oppose the war at its outbreak; its split came later, over conscription.

questions.stem: What was the result of the conscription referendums held in October 1916 and December 1917?
options: Both were carried, but conscription was never put into effect
The first was defeated and the second was carried narrowly
The first was carried, but the High Court struck down the law
Both were defeated, so the AIF remained a volunteer force
questions.explanation: Australians voted No on 28 October 1916 and again, by a wider margin, on 20 December 1917. The AIF stayed all-volunteer for the rest of the war.

questions.stem: What was the most immediate political consequence of the 1916 conscription campaign for the Labor Party?
options: Hughes resigned as prime minister and was replaced as Labor leader by anti-conscriptionist Frank Tudor
The Labor caucus voted to support conscription, and the anti-conscriptionists left the party
Hughes and his supporters left Labor and later formed the Nationalist Party with the Liberals
Labor reunited behind Hughes and won the 1917 election in a landslide on a Yes platform
questions.explanation: Labor's anti-conscription majority repudiated Hughes in November 1916. He walked out with his supporters, formed a National Labor government and in 1917 merged with the Liberals as the Nationalist Party, staying prime minister. Tudor led the Labor remnant in opposition.

questions.stem: In 1939 Robert Menzies broadcast that Australia was at war. On what basis did he say this?
options: Britain had declared war on Germany, and as a result Australia was also at war
Parliament had voted to declare war after Germany attacked Australian shipping
Australia had signed a treaty with Poland promising to defend its borders
The League of Nations had ordered its members to take military action
questions.explanation: Menzies told listeners that, because Germany persisted in invading Poland, Britain had declared war and Australia was therefore at war too. He treated Australia's involvement as following automatically from Britain's decision, as in 1914.

questions.stem: In December 1941 the Curtin government declared war on Japan in its own right rather than treating Britain's declaration as binding. Why do historians see this as significant?
options: It meant Australia could no longer receive help from British forces
It ended Australia's membership of the British Commonwealth
It showed Australia acting as an independent nation in foreign policy
It was the first time an Australian government had refused to support Britain
questions.explanation: Unlike 1914 and 1939, the Curtin government issued a separate declaration, marking a step towards an independent foreign policy. It did not break with Britain or the Commonwealth: the two remained allies throughout the war.

questions.stem: In a newspaper article in late December 1941, John Curtin wrote that Australia now 'looks to America'. What did he argue?
options: Britain should send its fleet to Australia so that the United States could defend Singapore
Australia should look to the United States without regret about its traditional ties to Britain
Australia should leave the Empire and sign a permanent alliance with the United States at once
Australian troops should be placed under American command in Europe rather than British
questions.explanation: Curtin argued that Australia would look to America in the Pacific war, free of any pangs about its traditional links with the United Kingdom. He did not propose leaving the Empire, and a formal alliance with the US came only with ANZUS in 1951.

questions.stem: Why did the Fall of Singapore on 15 February 1942 shock Australians so deeply?
options: It forced Australia to withdraw from the war against Germany
It exposed the failure of the British defence strategy Australia had relied on
It was the first time Australian troops had fought against Japanese forces
It led directly to a Japanese invasion of the Australian mainland
questions.explanation: Australia had relied on the 'Singapore strategy', the promise that a British fleet based there would protect it. The fall, with thousands of Australians of the 8th Division taken prisoner, showed Britain could not defend Australia. Australians had already fought the Japanese in Malaya, and no invasion of the mainland followed.

questions.stem: The Defence (Citizen Military Forces) Act 1943 is significant in the history of Australian conscription because it:
options: gave the government power to send conscripts to fight in Europe and the Middle East
ended compulsory service for home defence and made the militia an all-volunteer force
required a referendum before conscripts could be sent to New Guinea or other territories
let conscripted militia serve beyond Australian territory in a defined South-West Pacific Zone
questions.explanation: Curtin, who had campaigned against conscription in 1916–17, persuaded Labor to let militia conscripts serve in a defined zone of the South-West Pacific. They could not be sent to Europe or the Middle East, and no referendum was held.

questions.stem: Militia units, which included conscripts, fought on the Kokoda Track in 1942 before the 1943 Act was passed. How was this possible?
options: The United States commander in the Pacific had power to order Australian conscripts abroad
Papua was an Australian territory, where militia could already serve under the Defence Act
The government held a referendum in 1942 that approved overseas service for the militia
All the militiamen on the Kokoda Track had volunteered to transfer into the Second AIF
questions.explanation: The Defence Act allowed the militia to serve in Australia and its territories, and Papua was an Australian territory. The 1943 Act was needed to send them further, into a wider zone of the South-West Pacific.

questions.stem: Which idea best explains the enthusiasm with which many Australians greeted the outbreak of war in 1914?
options: A belief that Germany was about to invade the Australian mainland
Widespread support for pacifism among the Australian labour movement
A desire to gain colonies in Africa as a reward for Australian service
Loyalty to the British Empire and a sense of shared British identity
questions.explanation: In 1914 most Australians saw themselves as British, and duty to the Empire drove much early enlistment. Pacifism was a minority view, and fear of a German invasion of Australia was not a major motive.

questions.stem: The Anzac legend that grew after the Gallipoli landing in 1915 is best described as:
options: an official government policy that made enlistment in the AIF compulsory for single men in each state
a British army doctrine that Australian commanders adopted for fighting on the Western Front
a peace movement formed by returned soldiers who opposed further Australian involvement in war
a set of ideas about an Australian character, such as mateship and endurance, linked to nationhood
questions.explanation: The Anzac legend, promoted by writers such as Charles Bean, presented Australian soldiers as resourceful, egalitarian and loyal to their mates, and linked their sacrifice to the birth of a nation. It combined a developing Australian identity with continuing loyalty to the Empire.

questions.stem: Supporters of the Defence Act 1909 argued for compulsory military training mainly because they:
options: feared an attack on a thinly populated Australia, particularly from Asia
wanted a large army ready to fight in Europe in a future war against Germany
believed military drill would reduce support for trade unions among young men
hoped to replace the Royal Navy's protection with an Australian fleet
questions.explanation: Fear of invasion, especially after Japan's victory over Russia in 1905, shaped the argument for compulsory training for home defence. The scheme did not provide troops for Europe, and naval defence was handled separately with the creation of the Royal Australian Navy.

questions.stem: A group of Melbourne women formed the Women's Peace Army in 1915. Which idea most shaped its campaigning?
options: Imperial loyalty, the duty of Australians to aid Britain with men and money
Home defence, the view that the AIF should be kept in Australia to guard the coast
Militarism, the belief that strong armed forces are the basis of national greatness
Pacifism, the belief that war is wrong and disputes should be settled peacefully
questions.explanation: Led by figures such as Vida Goldstein, Cecilia John and Adela Pankhurst, the Women's Peace Army opposed the war and campaigned against conscription. Its pacifism set it against conservative women's groups that backed conscription.

questions.stem: A 1942 Australian government poster showed a Japanese soldier striding towards Australia across a map with the words 'He's coming south'. The idea this source drew on most directly was:
options: Australian independence, used to justify withdrawing troops from the Middle East
fear of invasion, used to urge Australians to commit fully to the war effort
loyalty to the Empire, used to recruit men for service with British forces in Africa
pacifism, used to persuade Australians to seek a negotiated peace with Japan
questions.explanation: The poster played on fear of a Japanese invasion after the fall of Singapore to boost the war effort at home. It is a useful source for official propaganda, though historians debate whether Japan actually planned to invade the mainland.

questions.stem: During World War Two, organisations such as the Australian Women's Army Service and the Women's Auxiliary Australian Air Force were created. What did this change reflect?
options: A peacetime decision to make the armed forces open equally to women
The government's response to a successful equal pay case in 1938
Wartime manpower needs opening military service roles to women
The admission of women to front-line combat units for the first time
questions.explanation: Labour shortages led to women's auxiliary services in the army, navy and air force, freeing men for combat. Women served in support roles such as signals, transport and clerical work, not combat, and most were demobilised after the war.

questions.stem: Archbishop Daniel Mannix was one of the best-known opponents of conscription. Which perspective did he represent most strongly?
options: Irish-Australian Catholic opinion, angered by Britain's response to the 1916 Easter Rising
Protestant clergy who believed conscription would protect the Empire from Catholic influence
Returned soldiers who argued that the AIF no longer needed reinforcements from Australia
Pacifist Quakers who refused all forms of military service on grounds of conscience
questions.explanation: Mannix, coadjutor and from 1917 Catholic Archbishop of Melbourne, called conscription a hateful thing and spoke for many working-class Irish Catholics. British executions after the Easter Rising deepened their resentment, so the debate took on a sectarian edge.

questions.stem: Opponents of Hughes during the conscription campaigns accused some Catholic leaders of disloyalty, while some Catholics saw Hughes as anti-Irish. A historian describing this debate would most likely use the term:
options: isolationism, the wish to avoid any involvement in overseas conflicts
federalism, the dispute over the powers of the states and the Commonwealth
socialism, the demand that the means of production be publicly owned
sectarianism, conflict shaped by divisions between Catholics and Protestants
questions.explanation: The conscription campaigns sharpened divisions between a largely Irish-Catholic community and a mostly Protestant establishment. The debate was not isolationist, since most anti-conscriptionists still supported the war effort through voluntary enlistment.

questions.stem: Why did many trade unionists and Labor supporters vote No in 1916 and 1917?
options: They feared conscription of men would lead to cheap labour and weaker wages and conditions
They believed Australia should withdraw completely from the war and recall the AIF
They wanted conscription delayed until the AIF had been reorganised by Australian officers
They objected that the referendums excluded women and returned soldiers from voting
questions.explanation: Many in the labour movement argued that conscripting men while leaving wealth untouched was unjust, and feared employers would replace absent workers with cheap or non-white labour. Most did not call for Australia to leave the war, and women and soldiers did vote.

questions.stem: 'The Blood Vote', a poem and leaflet used in the 1917 campaign, imagined a mother whose vote could send a man to his death. Which side used it, and to what effect?
options: The No side, to persuade women that a Yes vote would condemn men to die
The Yes side, to shame women whose sons had not yet volunteered for the AIF
The government, to explain the new censorship rules to women voters
The Yes side, to celebrate mothers whose sons had died at Gallipoli
questions.explanation: The anti-conscription campaign appealed directly to women, who could vote, by suggesting a Yes vote made them responsible for sending men to die. Both sides directed propaganda at women in 1916 and 1917.

questions.stem: Australian women's groups took different sides on conscription. Which pairing is accurate?
options: Both groups supported it, while only male trade unions campaigned for the No case
The Australian Women's National League supported it; the Women's Peace Army opposed it
The Women's Peace Army supported it; the Australian Women's National League opposed it
Both groups opposed it because women would have to replace conscripted workers
questions.explanation: The conservative Australian Women's National League backed Hughes and the Yes case, while the Women's Peace Army campaigned for No. The split shows that women's movements did not speak with one voice on the war.

questions.stem: Britain and New Zealand introduced conscription for overseas service in 1916 by passing laws in parliament, and Canada did so in 1917. How did the Australian debate differ?
options: Parliament passed a conscription law, but it was later struck down as invalid by the High Court
Conscription was introduced without debate because the Defence Act already allowed it
The question was decided by the governor-general on the advice of the British cabinet
The question was put to voters, who rejected it twice, so no conscription law was passed
questions.explanation: Hughes lacked a majority in the Senate for conscription and chose to seek popular approval. Australians rejected it twice, so the AIF stayed voluntary, while the other dominions' parliaments legislated for conscription.

questions.stem: During World War One, newspapers were stopped from publishing casualty details and anti-war views without approval. This censorship was mainly carried out under:
options: the National Security Act 1939
the Immigration Restriction Act 1901
the Defence (Citizen Military Forces) Act 1943
the War Precautions Act 1914
questions.explanation: The War Precautions Act gave the government sweeping powers to make regulations, including press censorship. The National Security Act was its World War Two counterpart.

questions.stem: In 1917 the Queensland Premier T. J. Ryan's anti-conscription speech was censored, and Commonwealth officials raided the Queensland Government Printing Office to seize copies of Hansard. What does this episode best illustrate?
options: The success of the War Precautions Act in uniting the states behind Hughes
The use of wartime powers to suppress opposition to the government's conscription case
The High Court's power to override state governments on questions of defence policy
The Queensland government's support for the Yes case in the 1917 referendum
questions.explanation: Hughes used the War Precautions Act against a state premier who opposed conscription, which many saw as an abuse of power. Ryan was a prominent leader of the No case, and Queensland voted No.

questions.stem: Under the War Precautions Act 1914, thousands of people classed as 'enemy aliens' were:
options: deported to Britain to be tried for treason
given land to farm under soldier settlement
interned in camps such as Holsworthy, near Sydney
conscripted into labour battalions sent to France
questions.explanation: People of German and Austro-Hungarian background, including many born in Australia or long settled here, could be interned in camps such as Holsworthy. German place names were also changed and German-language schools closed.

questions.stem: The 1917 General Strike in New South Wales began in railway workshops over the introduction of a time-card system. Which home-front pressure helped turn it into a strike of many industries?
options: Mass unemployment caused by conscription of workers
The banning of all trade unions under wartime law
Rising prices and falling real wages during the war
The introduction of petrol and clothing rationing
questions.explanation: Wartime inflation outpaced wages, and anger over the time-card system spread across many industries. Unions were not banned, rationing on that scale belonged to World War Two, and there was no conscription in World War One.

questions.stem: The Unlawful Associations Act 1916 was aimed mainly at which group?
options: The Industrial Workers of the World, a radical anti-war union
The Australian Women's National League, which supported conscription
The Returned Sailors and Soldiers Imperial League
German Lutheran congregations in South Australia
questions.explanation: The IWW opposed the war and conscription, and twelve of its members in Sydney were jailed in 1916. The Act made membership of the IWW illegal, showing how wartime law was used against radical dissent.

questions.stem: The Australian Red Cross and the Australian Comforts Fund depended largely on women's:
options: paid work in munitions factories run by the Commonwealth government
service as nurses in the front-line trenches at Gallipoli and in France
employment as clerks in the Department of Defence in Melbourne
voluntary work, such as knitting socks and packing parcels for soldiers
questions.explanation: Women's voluntary work raised money and sent comforts to soldiers on a huge scale during World War One. Australian nurses did serve overseas, but in hospitals and casualty clearing stations, not the trenches.

questions.stem: Which development shows the growth of Commonwealth power over the economy during World War Two?
options: The states were given control of wages through new state arbitration courts
The Commonwealth handed the running of the state railways over to private companies
The High Court ruled that the Commonwealth could not ration food or clothing
The Commonwealth took over the collection of income tax from the states in 1942
questions.explanation: Under uniform taxation the Commonwealth became the only collector of income tax, a wartime change that became permanent. Rationing, price controls and manpower direction under the National Security Act further increased its role.

questions.stem: Under the National Security Act 1939, the Manpower Directorate created in 1942 could:
options: conscript women for combat service in New Guinea and the islands
set the price of shares traded on the stock exchanges
release enemy aliens from internment to work on farms
direct civilians into essential jobs and stop them leaving them
questions.explanation: Manpower controls let the government direct labour to essential industries and restrict workers from changing jobs. Women were directed into civilian work, but none were conscripted for combat.

questions.stem: Which organisation was banned under National Security regulations in 1940?
options: The Communist Party of Australia
The Australian Labor Party
The Australian Council of Trade Unions
The Country Women's Association
questions.explanation: The Menzies government banned the Communist Party in 1940, when the Soviet Union was still in a pact with Nazi Germany. The ban was lifted in 1942, after the Soviet Union had joined the Allies.

questions.stem: In 1942 the Women's Employment Board set wages for women doing work previously done by men. A historian assessing change for working women would most accurately conclude that:
options: women won equal pay with men across all industries for the duration of the war
the Board lowered women's wages to free money for war spending
women's wartime wages were made permanent when the war ended in 1945
women's wages rose in many jobs, but the principle of equal pay was not established
questions.explanation: The Board often set women's rates well above the usual female rate, but generally still below men's, and only for the war. After 1945 many women left or were pushed out of these jobs, so the change was significant but limited.

questions.stem: Dunera, Hay and Tatura are linked in Australian World War Two history because they relate to:
options: factories run by the Manpower Directorate
internment of people classed as enemy aliens
battles fought by the militia in New Guinea
camps for American servicemen on leave
questions.explanation: The Dunera brought mostly Jewish refugees deported from Britain in 1940, who were interned at Hay; Tatura in Victoria held internees and prisoners of war. Italian, German and Japanese residents were also interned.

questions.stem: Defence rules in World War One excluded men 'not substantially of European origin or descent'. How did this affect Aboriginal men who wished to enlist?
options: They were allowed to enlist only in segregated Aboriginal battalions
They were required to enlist under the Defence Act 1909 like other men
Many were rejected, though some enlisted and restrictions were eased in 1917
They were conscripted into labour units because they were barred from fighting
questions.explanation: The rule kept many Aboriginal men out, yet some enlisted anyway, and from 1917 recruiters could accept men with one parent of European descent. Aboriginal soldiers served in ordinary units alongside other soldiers; there were no segregated battalions.

questions.stem: Aboriginal soldiers returning from World War One were largely denied land under soldier settlement schemes and still lived under protection laws in most states. What does this suggest about continuity and change?
options: Protection laws were repealed in recognition of Aboriginal military service
Aboriginal veterans received larger soldier settlement blocks than other veterans
Service in the AIF did not bring equal rights or treatment for Aboriginal veterans
Military service quickly won Aboriginal veterans full citizenship and voting rights
questions.explanation: Aboriginal soldiers often experienced equality in the ranks, but at home discrimination continued: most were left out of soldier settlement and remained under protection board control. Equal treatment in uniform did not change their status as citizens.

questions.stem: During World War Two the Torres Strait Light Infantry Battalion defended the Torres Strait. What was a major grievance of its Torres Strait Islander soldiers?
options: They were paid much less than white soldiers doing the same service
They were forbidden to serve in the Torres Strait and sent to the Middle East
They were conscripted while white Australians in the region were exempt
They were placed under the command of the United States Army
questions.explanation: Torres Strait Islander soldiers received a fraction of white soldiers' pay, which led to a protest strike at the end of 1943 and only a partial increase. Compensation for the underpayment was paid decades later.

questions.stem: Reg Saunders is remembered in Australian military history as:
options: the first Aboriginal man elected to federal parliament after World War Two
the first Aboriginal man commissioned as an officer in the Australian Army
the commander of the Torres Strait Light Infantry Battalion in 1942–43
the leader of the Aboriginal Day of Mourning protest in Sydney in 1938
questions.explanation: Saunders, a Gunditjmara man from Victoria, fought in North Africa, Greece, Crete and New Guinea and was commissioned in 1944. He later served as a company commander in the Korean War.

questions.stem: What was the main aim of soldier settlement schemes after World War One?
options: To house returned soldiers in new public flats in the cities
To give returned servicemen farm land as a reward and a livelihood
To settle new British migrants on farm land left vacant by enlisted men
To return Aboriginal land taken during the war to its owners
questions.explanation: Soldier settlement put returned men on small farms. Many blocks failed because they were too small or on poor land, the settlers lacked experience, and prices fell in the 1920s.

questions.stem: Which comparison of repatriation after the two world wars is most accurate?
options: After World War Two, the government abolished all special support for veterans
After both wars, veterans' support was left entirely to charities such as the Red Cross
After World War Two, retraining and education schemes added to land settlement
After World War One, returned men received free university education and housing
questions.explanation: The Commonwealth Reconstruction Training Scheme after 1945 gave many ex-service men and women trade and university training, alongside war service homes and a more cautious land settlement scheme. After World War One, support centred on pensions, the Repatriation Department and soldier settlement.

questions.stem: A historian argues that the world wars brought 'lasting change to the role of the Commonwealth, but only temporary change for women workers'. Which evidence best supports both parts of this claim?
options: Uniform income tax continued after 1945, while many women lost wartime jobs to returning men
The War Precautions Act was repealed in 1920, while women gained equal pay in 1945
The National Security Act remained in force until the 1970s, while women entered combat units
Soldier settlement continued after 1945, while women's auxiliary services were made permanent
questions.explanation: The Commonwealth kept its monopoly on income tax and its expanded social services after 1945, a lasting change. Women's wartime gains in employment and wages were largely reversed as men returned. Equal pay and women's combat roles came much later.

questions.stem: Which statement best evaluates continuity in Australian attitudes to defence between 1909 and 1945?
options: Australians accepted compulsory service to defend Australia but long resisted conscription for overseas service
Australians rejected all forms of compulsory service until the threat from Japan in 1941
Australians supported conscription for overseas service throughout, but Britain would not allow it
Australians consistently wanted to fight only in Europe and refused to defend the Pacific
questions.explanation: Compulsory training for home defence was accepted from 1911, and compulsory militia service returned in 1939–40, but overseas conscription was rejected in 1916 and 1917 and limited to a defined zone in 1943. The distinction between home defence and service abroad runs through the whole period.
